title: When Combinations of Humans and AI Are Useful: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
author: Michelle Vaccaro · Abdullah Almaatouq · Thomas Malone

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Benchmark governance: High scores may lack workplace meaning
st.an: The supplied source material contains only bibliographic references and no substantive findings, arguments or recommendations. It therefore provides insufficient evidence to determine whether the source accepts, extends or challenges the cluster’s proposition about benchmark scores and workplace suitability.

st.t: Creative diversity: Individual gains can homogenise groups
st.an: The source supports the narrower claim that creation tasks show more promising human–AI synergy than decision tasks, while stressing evidentiary limits. It does not assess collective diversity, homogenisation, or persona-based mitigation, so its position on the cluster’s principal quality–diversity proposition cannot be determined.
qs: And in these cases we found that the average effect size for human-AI synergy was positive and significantly greater than that for decision tasks.
As the human-AI collaboration literature develops, we hope future work can identify more factors that influence human-AI synergy and assess the interactions among them.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The supplied evidence shows that the source quantitatively analyses moderators of human–AI synergy and augmentation, which is relevant to the cluster’s emphasis on task, user and workflow conditions. However, the excerpts do not disclose effect directions or substantive conclusions, and provide no legal-specific findings on verification, competence, workflow redesign or replacement. Its position relative to the cluster therefore cannot be determined.
qs: The symbols in front of the moderator indicate if there is a statistically significant difference between the subgroups for human-AI synergy (*) and human augmentation (∧ ).

st.t: Task allocation: AI redistributes skill and responsibility
st.an: The EntityClusterSummary contains no title, description, key points or quotations. There is therefore no evidence from this source to determine its position on the cluster’s proposition that AI’s effects depend on task allocation, collaboration design and governance.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source strongly accepts the cluster’s central proposition and materially strengthens it with meta-analytic evidence: human–AI systems augment humans on average but do not generally outperform the better standalone component, with outcomes varying by task type, relative human/AI capability and workflow design. It directly supports selective deployment and adds a concrete design principle—allocate subtasks to whichever partner has the comparative advantage—while qualifying that evidence on predetermined task allocation remains sparse.
qs: In other words, the human-AI systems we analyzed were, on average, better than humans alone but not better than both humans alone and AI alone.

Additionally, as discussed in [33], human-AI synergy requires that humans be better at some parts of a task, AI be better at other parts of the task, and the system as a whole be good at appropriately allocating subtasks to whichever partner is best for that subtask.

st.t: Practical productivity: AI can save or consume time
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s insistence on measuring practical performance rather than inferring productivity from AI capability or adoption. It provides a rigorous three-condition comparison—human alone, AI alone, and human–AI collaboration—and codes task, participant, model and metric differences as potential moderators. However, the supplied excerpts contain methods only, so they do not establish whether collaboration improves performance or saves time.
qs: To calculate our primary outcome of interest – the effect of combining human and artificial intelligence on task performance – we recorded the averages and standard deviations of the task performance of the human alone, the AI alone, and the human and AI working with each other, as well as the number of subjects in each of these conditions (see S1.3 for details).

We considered and coded for multiple potential moderators of human-AI performance, namely: (1) publication date (2) pre-registration status (3) experimental design (4) data type (5) task type (6) task output (7) AI type (8) AI explanation (9) AI confidence (10) participant type and (11) performance metric.

kp.k: Synergy requires outperforming both standalone humans and AI
kp.d: The authors distinguish human-AI synergy, which requires the combination to outperform the better standalone participant, from human augmentation, which requires only improvement over humans alone. They argue that augmentation remains an appropriate objective when legal, ethical, safety or human-value considerations prevent full automation. This is a cross-domain framework rather than a finding about legal services specifically.
qs: Definition 1 (Human-AI Synergy). The human-AI group outperforms both the human and the AI alone.
Definition 2 (Human Augmentation). The human-AI group outperforms the human alone.
This measure can serve important purposes in contexts for which full automation cannot happen for legal, ethical, or safety reasons and in cases when AI does not align with human values.

kp.d: The pre-registered review identified 74 eligible papers from 5126 papers, yielding 106 experiments and 370 unique effect sizes. The search covered publications from January 1, 2020 to June 30, 2023 and required quantitative performance measures for humans alone, AI alone and their combination. The authors used standardized Hedges’ g and a three-level random-effects model to account for dependent effect sizes within experiments.
qs: These papers reported the results of 106 unique experiments, and many of the experiments had multiple conditions, so we collected a total of 370 unique effect sizes measuring the impact of human-AI collaboration on task performance.
To focus on current forms of artificial intelligence, we limited the search to studies published between January 1, 2020 and June 30, 2023.
We thus adopted a three-level meta-analytic model in which effect sizes are nested within experiments, so we explicitly took the dependencies in our data into account in the model [62, 63].

kp.k: Combinations improve humans but underperform the better standalone participant
kp.d: Across the reviewed experiments, the pooled synergy effect was significantly negative: g = −0.23, 95% CI −0.39 to −0.07, p = 0.005. By contrast, human augmentation was positive: g = 0.64, 95% CI 0.53 to 0.74. The finding is underperformance relative to the better standalone baseline, not a claim that combinations generally perform worse than both humans and AI separately. The authors limit this comparison to the performance dimensions measured.
qs: First, we found that, on average, human-AI combinations performed significantly worse than the best of humans or AI alone (Hedges’ g = −0.23, 95% confidence interval −0.39 to −0.07).
In other words, the human-AI systems we analyzed were, on average, better than humans alone but not better than both humans alone and AI alone.

kp.k: Creation tasks show more promise than decision tasks
kp.d: Task type significantly moderated synergy (p = 0.006). Decision tasks had a significantly negative pooled effect, g = −0.27, 95% CI −0.44 to −0.10; creation tasks had a positive but statistically nonsignificant effect, g = 0.19, 95% CI −0.09 to 0.48, p = 0.180. Creation tasks contributed only 34 effect sizes. Thus, the significant result is the difference between task categories, not demonstrated positive synergy within creation tasks.
qs: Even though the average performance gains for creation tasks were not significantly different from 0 (presumably because of the relatively small sample size of n = 34), the difference between losses for decision tasks and gains for creation tasks was statistically significant.
Far fewer come from creation tasks, which entail some kind of open-ended response (n = 34, 9%).

kp.k: Relative standalone performance strongly moderates collaboration outcomes
kp.d: In the main moderator analysis, combinations achieved positive synergy when humans outperformed AI alone: g = 0.46, with the main text reporting 95% CI 0.28 to 0.66. When AI outperformed humans alone, combinations underperformed AI: g = −0.54, 95% CI −0.71 to −0.37. Nevertheless, this latter group showed substantial augmentation relative to humans alone, g = 0.74, 95% CI 0.63 to 0.85. Separately fitted subgroup models in Table S4 report synergy estimates of 0.39 and −0.53, respectively.
qs: Interestingly, when the AI alone outperformed the human alone, substantial performance losses occurred in the human-AI systems.
When the human outperformed the AI alone, however, performance gains occurred in the human-AI systems.
When the AI outperformed the human alone, greater performance gains tended to occur in the human-AI systems relative to the human alone

kp.k: Trust calibration is a proposed mechanism, not established causation
kp.d: More than 95% of the reviewed systems gave humans the final decision after AI input. The authors hypothesize that humans who perform better overall may also judge more effectively when to accept AI advice. They illustrate this using Cabrera, Perer and Hong: fake-review detection achieved 73% accuracy for AI, 55% for humans and 69% for the combination; bird classification achieved 73%, 81% and 90%, respectively. These examples support the reported pattern, while the explanation remains explicitly hypothetical.
qs: Most (>95%) of the human-AI systems in our data set involved humans making the final decisions after receiving input from the AI algorithms.

In these cases, one potential explanation of our result is that, when the humans are better than the algorithms overall, they are also better at deciding in which cases to trust their own opinions and in which to rely more on the algorithm’s opinions.

kp.k: Several popular collaboration features show no significant moderation
kp.d: Explanations, confidence information, participant type and predetermined division of labor were not statistically significant moderators of either synergy or augmentation. AI type and publication year significantly moderated synergy, while experimental design moderated augmentation. The authors recommend greater research attention to baseline capabilities, task type and process design; the nonsignificant results do not establish that these features never matter in particular settings.
qs: The remaining moderators we investigated were not statistically significant for human-AI synergy or human augmentation (explanation, confidence, participant type, division of labor).
But we found that both factors significantly affected human-AI performance.

kp.k: Complementary task allocation is promising but sparsely tested
kp.d: Only three experiments, contributing four effect sizes, tested predetermined delegation of separate subtasks. Their pooled synergy estimate was positive but nonsignificant: g = 0.22, 95% CI −0.42 to 0.87, p = 0.494. The authors hypothesize that creation tasks benefit from combining human creativity, knowledge or insight with AI generation of routine content. They advocate allocating work according to complementary strengths, rather than assuming that having humans make final decisions automatically improves performance.
qs: Only 3 of the 100+ experiments in our analysis explore such processes with a pre-determined delegation of separate sub-tasks to humans and AI.

We hypothesize that this advantage for creation tasks occurs because even when creation tasks require the use of creativity, knowledge, or insight for which humans perform better, they often also involve substantial amounts of somewhat routine generation of additional content that AI can perform as well or better than humans.
In general, to effectively use AI in practice, it may be just as important to design innovative processes for how to combine humans and AI as it is to design innovative technologies [53].

kp.k: Delegation examples include both gains and losses
kp.d: The supplement reports that Lee et al.’s rehabilitation assessment system combined therapist feedback with AI assessment to achieve 93% accuracy, versus 75% for therapists and 87% for AI alone. Hemmer et al.’s image-classification system delegated cases using AI confidence and predicted human confidence, achieving 84%, versus 67% for humans and 75% for AI. Conversely, Lai et al.’s AI-summary post-editing workflow scored 5.5/7, below humans alone at 5.8/7, although above AI alone at 4.7/7. These are findings from cited experiments, not universal delegation effects.
qs: These authors find that the human-AI system outperforms the human alone and AI alone (84% accuracy versus 67% and 75%, respectively).
They find, however, that the human alone produces higher quality summaries (5.8/7) than both the AI alone (4.7/7) and the human-AI combination (5.5/7).
So this particular task allocation does not lead to human-AI synergy.

kp.k: Generative-AI studies need an AI-only performance baseline
kp.d: The authors identify creation tasks as a promising research direction, while noting that much generative-AI research measures attitudes or user experience rather than task performance. Studies comparing only humans with assisted humans cannot establish synergy because AI alone might outperform both. They recommend studying diverse tasks and reporting all three baselines.
qs: This limitation makes evaluating human-AI synergy difficult as the AI alone may be able to perform the task at a higher quality and speed than the participants involved in the experiment, typically crowdworkers.
We thus need studies that further explore human-AI collaboration across diverse tasks while reporting the performance of the human alone, AI alone, and human-AI system.

kp.k: Evaluation should include costs, time and consequential errors
kp.d: The authors argue that overall accuracy alone can omit important benefits or harms. In high-stakes applications, including radiology and bail predictions, human involvement may remain desirable if it reduces rare, especially costly errors, even when AI is more accurate and less expensive on average. This is a conditional recommendation, not evidence that humans consistently reduce such errors. They propose composite error-cost measures and evaluation incorporating completion time and financial cost.
qs: In these cases, even if AI can, on average, perform a task more accurately and less expensively than humans, it may still be desirable to include humans in the process if the humans are able to reduce the number of rare but very undesirable errors.

In general, we encourage researchers to develop, employ, and report more robust metrics that take into account factors such as task completion time, financial cost, and the practical implications of different types of errors.

kp.k: High heterogeneity and selection constrain generalization
kp.d: Heterogeneity was substantial: I² = 97.7% for synergy and 93.8% for augmentation. The review excludes tasks that humans or AI cannot perform alone, and the authors caution that studied tasks, participants and workflows may not represent practical deployments. Differences in participant populations, measurement error and study quality also constrain comparisons. Much heterogeneity remains unexplained, and there were too few studies to detect hypothesized interaction effects.
qs: We can, however, imagine tasks that a human and / or AI cannot perform alone but can when working with the other. Our analysis does not include such studies.

Fourth, our results only apply to the tasks, processes, and subject pools that researchers have chosen to study, and these configurations may not be representative of the ways human-AI systems are configured in practical uses of AI outside of the laboratory.
The moderators we investigate account for some of this heterogeneity, but much remains unexplained.

kp.k: Publication-bias findings differ between synergy and augmentation
kp.d: The detailed bias tests found no evidence of publication bias for synergy: Egger’s p = 0.438 and rank-correlation p = 0.121. However, they found potential bias favoring positive human-augmentation results: Egger’s p = 0.002 and rank-correlation p reported as 0.000. No bias correction was applied. Sensitivity checks using alternative clustering, outlier exclusion, leave-one-out analyses and exclusion of estimated data produced similar overall effects. The augmentation-specific warning qualifies the discussion’s broader statement about not finding publication bias.
qs: Importantly, however, we do find potential evidence of publication bias in favor of studies that report results in which the human-AI system outperforms the human alone (human augmentation).
Note that we did not try to correct for potential publication bias to preserve the integrity of the original data and maintain transparency in our reporting.

kp.k: Standardized reporting could improve cumulative collaboration research
kp.d: The authors recommend commensurability criteria covering benchmark tasks, quality thresholds, participant incentives, process types and evaluation metrics for all three performance conditions. They also propose an open repository containing raw data, code, outputs, interaction logs and documentation to facilitate replication and synthesis. Predictive models for context-specific system design are presented as a possible future use, not an achieved result.
qs: As researchers continue to study human-AI collaboration, we also urge the field to develop a set of commensurability criteria, which can facilitate more systematic comparisons across studies and help us track progress in finding areas of human-AI synergy.
This centralized database would host the studies’ raw data, code, system outputs, interaction logs, and detailed documentation, adhering to the proposed reporting guidelines.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Vaccaro, Almaatouq and Malone find that human–AI combinations improve human performance on average, but underperform the better of humans or AI alone; collaboration outcomes depend on task type and relative standalone performance.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain study of human–AI task performance, not a legal-services market forecast. The authors distinguish human augmentation, measured against humans alone, from synergy, measured against whichever standalone participant performs best. The pooled augmentation effect is g = 0.64 (95% CI 0.53 to 0.74), whereas the synergy effect is g = −0.23 (95% CI −0.39 to −0.07). This does not mean combinations generally underperform both standalone alternatives. Decision tasks show significantly negative synergy (g = −0.27); creation tasks show a positive but individually nonsignificant estimate (g = 0.19), with a significant difference between task types. When humans outperform AI alone, the moderator analysis finds positive synergy (g = 0.46); when AI outperforms humans alone, it finds losses against AI alone (g = −0.54). The authors hypothesize that stronger human performers can better decide when to rely on AI and that creation tasks permit complementary contributions. These mechanisms are proposed explanations, not established causal findings. Explanations, displayed confidence, participant type and predetermined division of labor were not statistically significant moderators. The authors recommend studying creation tasks and better allocation of subtasks rather than assuming human involvement automatically improves the best available performance.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims rest on a preregistered systematic review and multilevel meta-analysis of 370 effect sizes from 106 experiments in 74 papers, supplemented by illustrative experiments and explicitly tentative explanations.
pts.d: The authors screened 5,126 papers and required quantitative human-only, AI-only and combined-system performance. They used standardized Hedges’ g, a three-level random-effects model, robust variance estimation and separate moderator meta-regressions. Sensitivity analyses using different clustering, excluding outliers, omitting individual effects, experiments or papers, and excluding estimated data yielded similar overall findings. Heterogeneity was substantial: I² = 97.7% for synergy and 93.8% for augmentation. Publication-bias tests did not detect bias for synergy but did indicate potential bias favoring positive human-augmentation findings; the authors did not adjust for that potential bias. Their recommendation to allocate complementary subtasks has limited direct evidence: only three experiments, yielding four effect sizes, tested predetermined division of labor, with pooled synergy g = 0.22 (95% CI −0.42 to 0.87; p = 0.494). Illustrative studies discussed by the authors include complementary rehabilitation assessment and image-classification workflows, but also a summarization workflow in which human editing of AI summaries did not outperform human-only writing.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The findings concern experiments published from January 2020 through June 2023; future improvements are framed as research possibilities without a delivery date.
pts.d: The search was conducted in July 2023, and the supplied preprint version is dated 29 October 2024. The evidence concerns selected experimental tasks, participants, AI systems and interaction processes, not all practical deployments or subsequent models. Eligibility required standalone human, standalone AI and combined performance, excluding tasks that could only be performed collaboratively. More than 95% of the studied systems involved humans making final decisions after AI input. The results are conditional on the performance dimensions measured, which often omit time, financial costs and the differing consequences of errors. The authors therefore do not recommend universal automation: human augmentation remains relevant where legal, ethical or safety constraints prevent it, and human involvement may be desirable if it reduces rare, costly errors. They describe possible improvement in synergy over publication years as suggestive, not assured or rapid.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected groups are people using AI for decisions and creation, organizations designing collaborative workflows, researchers evaluating those workflows, and people exposed to consequential decisions.
pts.d: The experiments include doctors, crowdworkers and students, rather than a defined sample of lawyers or law firms. Decision-makers may improve against their own unaided performance while still lowering performance relative to a stronger standalone AI. Content creators are identified as a promising, but not conclusively demonstrated, setting for synergy. Researchers and organizational designers are encouraged to compare all three performance baselines, investigate complementary task allocation and evaluate costs, completion time and error consequences. The public may benefit from human involvement in high-stakes settings, such as radiology and bail prediction, if it reduces rare severe errors. Although law appears in the introduction as a field using AI, the source does not establish lawyer-specific effects or make concrete claims about legal employment, staffing structures, pricing, firm competition or access to justice.
